lessons.title: The Earth's Atmosphere Through Time
lessons.description: How the atmosphere changed over 4.5 billion years to today's mix.
lessons.content_html:
A Planet Transformed

Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. For most of that time, its atmosphere looked nothing like the air we breathe today. Understanding how it changed — and what drove those changes — is one of the most revealing stories in science, because it shows how life and chemistry have shaped each other over geological time.

Key Fact

Today’s atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and about 1% other gases including argon and a small but significant amount of carbon dioxide. This composition has been roughly stable for around 200 million years.

The Early Atmosphere — A Volcanic World

When Earth first formed, there was no free oxygen in the atmosphere at all. Intense volcanic outgassing during the first billion years or so produced a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)), with water vapour, nitrogen, methane and ammonia. This mix is similar to the present-day atmospheres of Venus and Mars — a useful comparison that helps scientists reason about what Earth’s early conditions were like.

As the planet cooled, water vapour condensed and fell as rain, forming the early oceans over hundreds of millions of years. At the same time, much of the carbon dioxide dissolved into those oceans or was locked away into sedimentary rocks and the shells and skeletons of early marine organisms.

Scientists cannot observe the early atmosphere directly — they must reason from indirect evidence. Key sources include: the composition of ancient volcanic gases (which match the pattern of nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour); analysis of chemical signatures in ancient rocks; and comparison with the present-day atmospheres of Mars and Venus, which did not undergo the same biological transformation that Earth did. This is a good example of how scientists build a model from multiple, independent lines of evidence rather than a single direct measurement.

The Rise of Oxygen — A Biological Revolution

The dramatic increase in atmospheric oxygen was driven by photosynthesis. Early photosynthetic organisms — including cyanobacteria and algae — evolved in the oceans and began releasing oxygen as a waste product. Over billions of years, this oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere, gradually replacing the carbon dioxide-rich conditions of the early Earth.

The oxygen increase had two major secondary effects. First, it enabled the evolution of aerobic (oxygen-using) organisms that could release far more energy from food than anaerobic life. Second, high-energy ultraviolet radiation from the Sun converted some oxygen molecules (\(O_2\)) into ozone (\(O_3\)), forming the ozone layer. This layer absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful UV radiation, which allowed life to colonise the land surface.

Key Fact

Carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere by two processes: dissolving in the oceans (and being incorporated into carbonate rocks and shells), and being used up by photosynthetic organisms. The biological route is why CO₂ is now only a tiny fraction of the atmosphere.

Stage 1 — Volcanic outgassing: Eruptions release a mixture of carbon dioxide, water vapour, nitrogen, methane and ammonia. No free oxygen present.

Stage 2 — Ocean formation: As Earth cools, water vapour condenses into rain and seas. Carbon dioxide begins dissolving and is trapped in carbonate rocks.

Stage 3 — Photosynthesis begins: Early life evolves and starts removing \(CO_2\) from the air, releasing \(O_2\). Oxygen levels rise slowly over hundreds of millions of years.

Stage 4 — Ozone layer forms: Rising oxygen allows an ozone layer to develop, shielding the surface from UV radiation. More complex life evolves and colonises land.

Stage 5 — Modern atmosphere established: Roughly 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~0.04% carbon dioxide. This balance has been broadly stable for around 200 million years — though human activity is now altering the concentration of carbon dioxide.

Nitrogen — The Quiet Majority

Nitrogen makes up nearly four-fifths of the atmosphere, yet it is relatively unreactive under ordinary conditions. It was released by volcanic activity and also produced as a byproduct of biological nitrogen cycling. Because nitrogen is so stable, it has not been consumed by chemical or biological reactions at anywhere near the rate that carbon dioxide was, so it has accumulated to become the dominant gas in the atmosphere over geological time.

The Ozone Layer — A Shield for Life on Land

One of the most significant consequences of rising oxygen was the formation of the ozone layer. High in the atmosphere, ultraviolet radiation from the Sun converts oxygen molecules into ozone. This layer of ozone then absorbs much of the harmful UV radiation before it reaches the surface. Without the ozone layer, DNA damage from UV radiation would make survival on land extremely difficult. The ozone layer therefore represents a critical threshold in the history of life on Earth — once it was established, the colonisation of land became possible, driving a dramatic expansion in the diversity and complexity of life over hundreds of millions of years.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on the atmosphere often ask you to explain a change, not just describe it — so include the cause. For instance, saying “oxygen increased because photosynthesis released it” earns more marks than “oxygen increased over time.” Be careful with ancient atmospheric percentages: the spec does not give specific figures for the early atmosphere, so avoid inventing numbers. Only state the modern composition confidently (approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen). If a question asks about evidence, name the type of evidence (ancient rocks, comparison with other planets) rather than making up specific studies.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The early atmosphere was produced by volcanic outgassing and was dominated by carbon dioxide and water vapour, with no free oxygen.
  • Photosynthesis by early organisms was the main driver of rising oxygen levels; carbon dioxide was also removed by dissolving in the oceans and forming carbonate rocks.
  • Today’s atmosphere (approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~0.04% carbon dioxide) has been broadly stable for around 200 million years, and the ozone layer it supports makes complex land life possible.

lessons.title: Energy in Chemical Reactions
lessons.description: Endothermic and exothermic reactions, energy profiles, and bond energies explained.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Is Always Transferred

Every chemical reaction involves an energy transfer. Energy is never created or destroyed — it is transferred between the reacting chemicals (the system) and the surroundings. Whether a reaction heats up or cools down its environment tells you which direction that transfer goes. This idea underpins everything from hand warmers to sports cold packs to the reactions that power living cells.

Key Fact

An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings rises. An endothermic reaction absorbs energy from the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings falls. A useful memory hook: EXO = energy EXits; ENDO = energy ENters.

Exothermic Reactions in Everyday Life

Combustion is the most familiar exothermic reaction — burning methane in a gas boiler, for example, transfers energy to the water in a central heating system. Neutralisation reactions (acid + alkali) are also exothermic; you can feel the flask warm up. Hand warmers that contain iron powder work by an exothermic oxidation reaction: iron slowly reacts with oxygen from the air and releases heat.

Endothermic Reactions in Everyday Life

Thermal decomposition reactions require continuous heating to proceed because they absorb energy from the surroundings. For example, heating copper carbonate causes it to decompose:

$$CuCO_3 \rightarrow CuO + CO_2$$

Sports injury cold packs are a familiar endothermic application: when the pack is activated, ammonium nitrate dissolves in water in an endothermic process, absorbing heat from the surroundings and cooling the injured area.

Activation Energy and Energy Profile Diagrams

Even an exothermic reaction needs an initial energy input to get started. This is called the activation energy — the energy needed to break existing bonds in the reactants so that new bonds can form in the products. Once a few bonds have been broken, the energy released by bond-making can sustain the reaction.

An energy profile diagram shows this graphically. The y-axis is energy; the x-axis is the progress of the reaction (sometimes called the reaction coordinate). The curve rises to a peak — the activation energy — before falling to the energy level of the products.

The activation energy arrow must start at the energy level of the reactants and end at the peak of the curve. A very common error is to draw the arrow from the y-axis or from the products — this scores no marks. Check: does your arrow begin on the reactant plateau and rise to the highest point on the curve?

For an exothermic reaction: the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants. The overall energy change (ΔH) is negative — energy has been released. For an endothermic reaction: the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants. The overall energy change is positive — energy has been absorbed.

Key Fact

On an energy profile diagram, the activation energy arrow always starts at the energy level of the reactants and points up to the peak. This is the most frequently penalised error in exams. Products below reactants = exothermic; products above reactants = endothermic.

Bond Breaking and Bond Making

The energy changes in reactions are explained at the bond level. Breaking chemical bonds always requires energy input — it is an endothermic process. Forming new chemical bonds always releases energy — it is an exothermic process. The overall energy change of a reaction depends on the balance between these two.

If the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants is less than the energy released when new bonds form in the products, the overall reaction is exothermic. If more energy is needed to break bonds than is released in making them, the reaction is endothermic.

Measuring Energy Changes in the Laboratory

A simple way to investigate whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic is to measure the temperature change of the solution. If you mix two chemicals in a polystyrene cup, the cup acts as a simple calorimeter. Recording the temperature before and after tells you the direction of energy transfer: a temperature rise confirms the reaction is exothermic; a fall confirms endothermic.

In practice, some energy is always lost to the surroundings even with insulation. Using a lid on the cup, taking readings quickly, and using a digital thermometer all reduce this systematic error. Being aware of the limitations of your equipment and method is part of working scientifically — acknowledging sources of error does not undermine a result, but it does show you understand the difference between what you measured and the true value.

bond energy values are given in kJ/mol and represent the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond. To calculate the overall energy change:

$$\Delta H = \text{Energy to break bonds in reactants} - \text{Energy released making bonds in products}$$

A negative result means exothermic (energy released); a positive result means endothermic (energy absorbed). Always set out the calculation clearly: list each bond broken with its energy, total them; list each bond made with its energy, total them; then subtract.

Worked example: For \(H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl\). Bond energies: H–H = 436 kJ/mol; Cl–Cl = 242 kJ/mol; H–Cl = 432 kJ/mol.
Energy to break bonds: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ/mol.
Energy released making bonds: 2 × 432 = 864 kJ/mol.
ΔH = 678 − 864 = −186 kJ/mol. Exothermic.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error on energy profile questions is drawing the activation energy arrow from the wrong starting point. Always start the arrow at the energy level of the reactants, not from the y-axis and not from the products. When asked to compare exothermic and endothermic profiles, comment explicitly on both the position of products relative to reactants and the size of the activation energy. In Higher-tier bond energy calculations, show every step: bonds broken (positive), bonds made (negative), then the difference — losing marks for missing units or skipped steps is avoidable.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings (temperature rises); endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings (temperature falls). All reactions require an activation energy to begin.
  • On an energy profile diagram, the activation energy arrow must start at the reactant energy level and rise to the peak of the curve — not from the y-axis or from the products.
  • Bond breaking always requires energy; bond making always releases energy. Whether a reaction is overall exothermic or endothermic depends on which process releases or absorbs more energy in total.

lessons.title: Climate Change — Evidence and Response
lessons.description: What the evidence shows about climate change and how scientists weigh competing claims.
lessons.content_html:
Science, Evidence and a Global Challenge

Climate change is one of the most significant scientific topics of our time — and one of the clearest examples of how scientists build confidence in a model by gathering many independent lines of evidence. This lesson focuses not just on the greenhouse effect as a concept, but on how scientists collect data, construct models, and evaluate claims about a complex system. Understanding that process is as important as knowing the facts.

The Greenhouse Effect — A Natural Mechanism

The Earth is warmed by solar radiation from the Sun. Much of this radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface. The surface then re-emits energy as infrared (heat) radiation. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb some of this outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions — including back towards the surface. This is the natural greenhouse effect, and without it, Earth’s average surface temperature would be far colder than it is.

Key Fact

The three main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)), methane (\(CH_4\)) and water vapour. Human activities have increased the concentration of carbon dioxide (burning fossil fuels, deforestation) and methane (intensive livestock farming, landfill).

The Evidence for Climate Change

The scientific case for human-caused climate change rests on multiple independent lines of evidence. No single measurement proves the case, but when many different datasets from different research groups around the world tell a consistent story, confidence in the conclusion grows. This is how science works: convergence of independent evidence increases the reliability of a model. If five different types of measurement — atmospheric gas records, ice core chemistry, satellite temperature data, ocean heat content, and glacier retreat observations — all point in the same direction, it becomes increasingly difficult to argue that all of them are wrong in the same way.

ice cores drilled from polar ice sheets contain tiny air bubbles that are samples of ancient atmosphere, trapped as each year’s snowfall compacted into ice. By analysing the gas composition of bubbles from different depths — which correspond to different time periods — scientists have reconstructed the history of atmospheric carbon dioxide and temperature stretching back hundreds of thousands of years. These records show a clear and tight correlation between \(CO_2\) concentration and global average temperature.

Since 1958, atmospheric \(CO_2\) has been measured continuously at a monitoring station at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, in work begun by Charles David Keeling. The resulting dataset — known as the Keeling Curve — shows a consistent, year-on-year rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide, with a seasonal oscillation caused by the annual growth cycle of plants in the northern hemisphere. This long-term dataset is one of the most powerful pieces of direct evidence for rising \(CO_2\).

Climate Models — Useful, But Not Certain

Scientists use climate models to project how the climate system may change in the future. These models are built on well-established physical laws and tested against past climate data. When a model accurately reproduces the climate record of the past century, scientists have greater confidence it can project future trends.

However, all models involve simplifications and uncertainties. Complex feedback loops (such as how changing ice cover affects how much sunlight is reflected) are difficult to represent exactly. Scientists communicate this uncertainty by presenting projections as ranges, not single values. Uncertainty in a model does not mean the model is wrong — it means we should treat its projections as estimates with upper and lower bounds rather than precise predictions.

Key Fact

Multiple independent lines of evidence support the conclusion that atmospheric \(CO_2\) is rising and contributing to warming: direct continuous measurements (the Keeling Curve), ice-core records of ancient atmospheric composition, and global surface temperature datasets from meteorological stations and satellites. Convergence across independent datasets strengthens confidence in the scientific consensus.

Weighing Evidence and Responding to Uncertainty

Because climate change involves complex systems and uncertain future projections, it raises important questions about how society responds to scientific evidence. The scientific consensus is that rising greenhouse gas concentrations are causing measurable warming and are likely to cause significant further changes. But deciding how to respond involves weighing risks and benefits, which brings in values and priorities alongside scientific knowledge.

For example, reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide emissions requires changes to energy production, transport and industry. These have economic and social costs in the short term. But failing to act also carries significant costs — the projected consequences of continued warming include rising sea levels, disruption to agriculture, water shortages in vulnerable regions, and more frequent extreme weather events. How to balance these competing concerns is ultimately a societal and political question, shaped by values and priorities. However, the underlying scientific evidence — gathered from ice cores, instrumental records, and climate modelling — defines the physical constraints within which any response must operate. Understanding both the science and its limits is essential for informed participation in these debates.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This topic often appears in extended-response questions that ask you to evaluate evidence or discuss how scientists reach conclusions. Remember the distinction: the question is asking about the process of science (how evidence is gathered, why multiple independent sources matter, what uncertainty in a model means) as much as the content. Avoid claiming specific numerical targets or percentages unless you are certain — instead, use qualitative language: “CO₂ concentrations have risen significantly since industrialisation” is safer than a fabricated figure. For risk-benefit questions, you must explicitly weigh the two sides rather than just listing them separately.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The greenhouse effect is a natural warming mechanism in which greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour) absorb and re-emit infrared radiation; human activity has increased the concentrations of these gases, enhancing the effect.
  • Evidence for climate change comes from multiple independent sources — including ice cores, the Keeling Curve and temperature records — and the convergence of these sources increases scientific confidence in the conclusion.
  • Climate models make projections with acknowledged uncertainty; scientific uncertainty does not invalidate a model but means projections should be presented as ranges. Responding to climate change involves balancing scientific evidence with societal risks and benefits.

practice_questions.text: Explain why scientists use multiple independent lines of evidence when building a case for climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: No single measurement proves the case (1); when independent datasets from different sources tell the same story, this convergence increases confidence in the conclusion (1); if different methods with different potential errors all agree, it is unlikely they are all wrong in the same way (1).
Secure: Two points with logical connection.
Developing: States that more evidence is better without explaining why convergence matters.
Emerging: Vague answer.

practice_questions.text: Compare the natural greenhouse effect with the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by human activity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both involve greenhouse gases absorbing infrared radiation emitted by the Earth (1). The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough to support life (1). The enhanced effect is caused by rising concentrations of CO₂ and methane from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and livestock farming (1). This traps more energy and raises global average temperatures beyond the natural baseline (1).
Secure: Natural vs enhanced clearly distinguished with two developed points.
Developing: One distinction made with partial development.
Emerging: Vague reference to more greenhouse gases.

practice_questions.text: A newspaper headline claims: 'Scientists cannot agree on climate change.' Evaluate this claim using your knowledge of how scientific evidence and models work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Challenges the claim — there is a strong scientific consensus that climate change is occurring and is linked to human greenhouse gas emissions (1). This consensus is based on convergence of multiple independent evidence sources (1). Uncertainty exists in the precise projections of future change, not in the fundamental conclusion (1). Uncertainty in a model does not mean disagreement among scientists about the direction of change (1). The distinction between reporting uncertainty in projections and claiming there is no consensus is important for public understanding of science (1).
Secure: Four points, logically connected.
Developing: Challenges claim with two supporting points.
Emerging: Challenges claim but minimal support.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the risks and benefits of reducing fossil fuel use as a response to climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits: reduces CO₂ emissions and slows further warming (1); reduces other pollutants such as particulates that harm health (1). Risks/costs: economic disruption to industries dependent on fossil fuels (1); transition costs for energy infrastructure (1). Weighing: the long-term projected consequences of continued warming (sea level rise, extreme weather, agricultural disruption) are likely to exceed the costs of transition (1); but the pace and distribution of costs and benefits is contested, and the most vulnerable communities often experience both the worst climate impacts and the greatest economic hardship from rapid transitions (1).
Secure: Both sides addressed with a weighing statement.
Developing: Lists risks and benefits without weighing.
Emerging: One-sided response.

glossary_terms.definition: Gases in the atmosphere, including carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, that absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and re-emit it in all directions, trapping heat.
The warming of the Earth's surface caused by greenhouse gases trapping infrared radiation; the natural effect is essential for life, but rising greenhouse gas concentrations are enhancing it.
A potent greenhouse gas released by livestock digestion, rice paddies, landfill sites and fossil fuel extraction, which traps heat more effectively than CO₂ per molecule over short timescales.
Cylinders of ice drilled from polar ice sheets that contain trapped ancient air bubbles, giving scientists a record of past atmospheric composition and temperature.
The long-running record of atmospheric CO₂ concentration measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, begun in 1958, showing a steady year-on-year rise in CO₂.
Computer simulations representing the physics and chemistry of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans, used to project how the climate will respond to changes in greenhouse gas concentrations.

lessons.title: Potable Water
lessons.description: How fresh water is treated to be safe to drink, and where supply comes from.
lessons.content_html:
Water We Can Drink

Access to clean drinking water is one of the most important applications of chemistry in everyday life. Potable water is not the same as pure water. Pure water contains only water molecules, but potable water contains small amounts of dissolved minerals and trace substances — these are acceptable at low levels and some are even beneficial. What matters is that the levels of dissolved substances and microorganisms are low enough to be safe.

In the UK, most potable water comes from surface water sources — rivers and reservoirs — and from groundwater stored in underground rock layers called aquifers. Rainfall replenishes these sources, so the UK’s temperate climate means supply is generally adequate, though regional variations mean some areas face greater pressure on water resources than others. Where fresh water sources are available, the treatment process described below is well established. In other parts of the world, particularly in arid or semi-arid regions, or on small islands without large freshwater reserves, different and more energy-intensive approaches are needed.

Key Fact

Treating fresh water to make it potable involves three main stages: filtration (removing particles and debris), sedimentation (allowing fine particles to settle), and sterilisation (killing microorganisms). Potable water is safe to drink — not chemically pure.

The Three Stages of Fresh Water Treatment

Filtration passes water through layers of gravel and sand. These filter beds trap large particles, suspended solids and some microorganisms. The water passes through progressively finer material, emerging much clearer. However, filtration alone does not remove all bacteria or dissolved contaminants — further treatment is needed.

Sedimentation allows fine particles that are too small to be caught by filtration to settle out under gravity in large settlement tanks. In some treatment plants, a coagulant chemical (such as aluminium sulfate) is added to cause tiny particles to clump together into larger flocs that settle more easily. The settled sludge is removed, and the cleaner water above it passes to the sterilisation stage.

Sterilisation kills bacteria and other harmful microorganisms that have survived filtration. The most common method in the UK is adding small, carefully controlled amounts of chlorine gas or a chlorine compound to the water. Ozone or ultraviolet (UV) light can also be used. These methods kill bacteria without making the water unsafe to drink at the concentrations used.

Desalination — Water from the Sea

In regions where fresh water is scarce, desalination can convert sea water into potable water. The two main methods are:

  • Distillation: Sea water is boiled; the steam is collected and condensed to give pure water, leaving the dissolved salts behind. This requires a large amount of energy to heat the water.
  • Reverse osmosis: Sea water is forced under high pressure through a semi-permeable membrane that allows water molecules through but blocks dissolved ions. This also requires significant energy to maintain the pressure.
Key Fact

Both desalination methods — distillation and reverse osmosis — produce potable water from sea water, but both require large amounts of energy. This makes desalination expensive and potentially high in carbon emissions unless powered by renewable energy. The UK relies on fresh water sources rather than desalination for most of its supply.

Analysing Water Samples (Required Practical)

The required practical for this topic involves analysing water samples to compare their purity. Students may test for the presence of dissolved ions using techniques such as flame tests (for metal ions) or precipitation reactions (e.g. adding silver nitrate to test for chloride ions). Comparing samples from different sources — such as tap water, bottled water and distilled water — illustrates how the composition of ‘potable’ water varies even within safe limits.

When planning such an investigation, the key variables are: the independent variable (which water sample is being tested), the dependent variable (the result of the chemical test), and the control variables (volume of sample used, concentration of reagents, temperature). Safety considerations include handling silver nitrate and chlorine-based solutions, which can irritate skin and eyes.

Waste Water Treatment

Potable water treatment is only one side of the equation. Water that has been used in homes, hospitals and industrial processes must also be treated before it can be safely returned to the environment. If untreated sewage or industrial waste water entered rivers and lakes directly, it would deplete oxygen levels, harm aquatic life and spread disease.

Waste water treatment typically involves several stages: screening (removing large solid objects), sedimentation (allowing solids to settle as sludge), biological treatment (using microorganisms to break down organic material in the water), and disinfection (to kill remaining pathogens before discharge). The sludge produced by sedimentation can sometimes be used as fertiliser after further treatment, illustrating how waste management and resource recovery can be combined.

Key Fact

Untreated waste water contains dissolved organic material, pathogens and sometimes toxic chemicals. Releasing it into natural water bodies depletes dissolved oxygen (harming aquatic life), spreads disease, and can contaminate drinking water sources. Treatment makes the water safe enough for environmental discharge.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing water treatment, use the correct sequence: filtration, then sedimentation, then sterilisation. Common errors include confusing ‘potable’ with ‘pure’ — always clarify that potable water contains some dissolved substances at safe levels, not zero dissolved solids. For questions about desalination, examiners expect you to name both methods (distillation and reverse osmosis) and to state that both require significant energy input, making them expensive. In required practical questions, name the independent and dependent variables and include at least one safety point.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Potable water is safe to drink but is not chemically pure — it contains low levels of dissolved substances. UK fresh water is treated by filtration, sedimentation and sterilisation (usually with chlorine, ozone or UV light).
  • Desalination (by distillation or reverse osmosis) can convert sea water to potable water but requires large energy inputs, making it expensive compared to treating fresh water sources.
  • The required practical involves analysing water samples to compare composition; a well-designed investigation identifies independent, dependent and control variables and includes appropriate safety measures.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'potable water'?
A) Water that contains no dissolved substances
B) Water that has been boiled
C) Water that is safe to drink, with sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microorganisms
D) Water that has only been filtered through sand
practice_questions.marks: C) Water that is safe to drink, with sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microorganisms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two methods that can be used to sterilise water during the treatment of fresh water.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two from: chlorine (or chlorine compounds) (1); ozone (1); ultraviolet light (UV) (1). Award 1 mark per correct method, max 2.
Secure: Two methods named correctly.
Developing: One method named.
Emerging: No creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: Describe how fresh water is treated to make it potable. Include the key stages in the correct order.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Filtration — passes water through gravel/sand filter beds to remove large particles (1); sedimentation — fine particles settle out in settlement tanks (1); sterilisation — chlorine/ozone/UV used to kill microorganisms (1).
Secure: All three stages named with brief explanation.
Developing: Two stages named correctly.
Emerging: One stage named.

practice_questions.text: Compare distillation and reverse osmosis as methods of desalination. Include in your answer one advantage and one disadvantage shared by both methods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both produce potable water from sea water (1); both require large amounts of energy, making them expensive (1); distillation works by boiling sea water and condensing the steam (1); reverse osmosis forces water under pressure through a semi-permeable membrane (1).
Secure: Both methods correctly described with shared disadvantage.
Developing: One method described accurately.
Emerging: Names one method only.

practice_questions.text: A student is investigating three water samples — tap water, sea water and distilled water — by testing for the presence of chloride ions using silver nitrate solution. Plan the investigation, identifying the key variables and one safety precaution.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Independent variable: which water sample is tested (1); dependent variable: whether a precipitate forms / the result of the silver nitrate test (1); control variables: volume of each sample used / concentration of silver nitrate / temperature (1); safety: silver nitrate stains skin and clothing and is an irritant — wear eye protection and gloves (1).
Secure: Variables correct plus safety.
Developing: Variables identified but safety missing or vice versa.
Emerging: General description without variable identification.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of desalination as a solution to water scarcity, considering both its advantages and its limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Advantages: desalination can produce potable water from sea water, making it valuable in regions with limited fresh water sources (1); it is not dependent on rainfall or river flow (1). Limitations: both distillation and reverse osmosis require large amounts of energy (1); this makes desalination expensive (1); if powered by fossil fuels, desalination itself contributes to greenhouse gas emissions, potentially worsening the climate change that is reducing water availability in some regions (1). Overall evaluation: desalination is an important technology in water-scarce regions but is not a universal solution — renewable energy-powered desalination would address the carbon cost but remains expensive at scale (1).
Secure: Four points with a weighing statement.
Developing: Lists advantages and limitations without weighing.
Emerging: One-sided response.

glossary_terms.definition: Water that is safe to drink, with sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts, bacteria and other contaminants; it is not chemically pure water.
The process of passing water through filter beds of gravel and sand to remove large particles, debris and some microorganisms.
The process of killing microorganisms in water to make it safe to drink, using chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet radiation.
The process of removing salt and other dissolved minerals from sea water or brackish water to produce potable water, using distillation or reverse osmosis.
A separation technique in which a liquid is boiled, the vapour collected and condensed back into a liquid, leaving non-volatile dissolved substances behind.
A desalination method in which sea water is forced under high pressure through a semi-permeable membrane that allows water molecules through but blocks dissolved ions.
